Goldman Sachs Research expects global music revenues to increase at 6.7% year-on-year in 2026 and at a compound rate of 5.8% per year between 2025 and 2035. “While growth is likely to moderate from the pace observed during the industry's streaming adoption phase, we continue to see a long runway for industry expansion supported by favorable consumer behavior and an increasingly diversified monetization model,” Laszczyk and Sheridan write. Paid streaming subscriptions are helping to shore up the outlook for recorded music. After three consecutive downgrades to its forecast for 2030 recorded music revenues, Goldman Sachs Research’s outlook for the segment this year reflects improvements in streaming revenue, physical revenue, and download and other digital revenue. articles.title: Emerging Market Credit Shows Resilience amid Energy Shock
articles.excerpt: When the Iran war triggered a surge in oil prices this year, many investors may have expected credit markets in the developing world to slide into a selloff. Instead, emerging market sovereign and corporate bonds weathered the shock with a newfound stability and solid performance for investors. The development is a key sign that emerging market credit is maturing into a resilient asset class, according to Anupam Damani, co-head and senior portfolio manager of emerging market debt at Goldman Sachs Asset Management. At the same time, investors are rethinking their approach to the market, which has trillions of dollars in outstanding debt. “Emerging market credit is now unrecognizable, and I mean that in a good way,” Damani says. “These bonds used to come with a crisis label, but this market is no longer monolithic. In my view, it has become a more diverse and resilient asset class, though risks remain.” To be sure, emerging market bonds run the gamut in terms of risk, and investors must be selective about what they trade in a marketplace with myriad issuers, she adds.

articles.title: The Rise of Healthcare Consumerism | Morgan Stanley
articles.excerpt: U.S. consumers are increasingly taking the lead in how they access and pay for healthcare, creating potential opportunities across biopharma and healthcare services. In the complex and costly U.S. healthcare system, patients are no longer just heeding drug ads to “Ask Your Doctor”—they’re going straight to the source. Policy changes and technological advances have given consumers more ways to directly choose the healthcare products and services that best suit their needs—including care, testing and medicines—as well as how they pay for them. The healthcare industry is adapting to this trend, potentially creating new opportunities for investors. In biopharma alone, the total direct-to-consumer cash-pay market could reach $26 billion at its peak. Eyeing that opportunity, many large-cap biopharma companies now offer direct-to-consumer platforms. Healthcare consumerism took root with the creation of Health Savings Accounts (HSAs) in 2003, followed by the growth of high-deductible health plans (HDHPs). These changes gave consumers more control over healthcare spending—but also shifted more of the costs and decisions to them.

articles.title: Winners and Losers From AI Agents | Morgan Stanley
articles.excerpt: As AI agents become more capable of making decisions and purchases on consumers’ behalf, Morgan Stanley Research examines which industries could benefit—and which face growing competitive pressure. The recent launch of powerful consumer AI agents has reignited debate over how artificial intelligence could disrupt industries ranging from retail and insurance to transportation and live entertainment. Unlike traditional AI tools that primarily answer questions, these agents can browse websites, complete forms, compare prices, make purchases and even help negotiate bills. Morgan Stanley Research estimates that roughly $30 trillion in consumer spending could be digitized through AI agents across online advertising, e-commerce, travel, food delivery, ridesharing, logistics, wearables and other sectors. The extent of the disruption will depend on how quickly consumers adopt AI agents and how effectively companies make money from agent-driven activity and transactions.

articles.excerpt: The AI buildout is accelerating, bringing binding constraints forward. We stay overweight U.S. equities and upgrade emerging market stocks to overweight but stay focused on opportunities driven by bottlenecks. Global government bond yields have surged through the summer. Higher yields have restored income opportunities, but only via a flexible approach. We prefer short-term bonds over long-term bonds with high sensitivity to interest rates. Asset-class buckets are a less useful starting point in a world shaped by mega forces. Infrastructure shows why: Its exposure to AI demand, energy security and fragmentation runs across markets and asset classes. The AI investment boom is having two broad impacts: lifting activity and earnings while absorbing more capital, power, materials and balance-sheet capacity. Heavy sovereign borrowing is adding to the demand for funding. The result is a higher cost of capital even as AI boosts growth. These developments reinforce our core Midyear Outlook themes: AI has the potential to deliver a sustained increase in growth and productivity, but that path to abundances runs through scarcity in capital, materials and labor.

Amid recent tech stock swings, we’re reconciling our longer-term AI conviction – which is a strategic overweight, as evidenced in our latest update to our capital market assumptions – with nearer-term caution – our tactical 6–12 month horizon view is neutral. The picture for U.S. stocks depends on how you measure valuations. One measure suggests stocks are almost as expensive as they were during the dot-com bubble. Another paints a less extreme picture. But that's because investors are counting on strong earnings growth. Whether AI can deliver that growth is still an open question. For one, cheaper computing could squeeze profits for AI suppliers. Meanwhile, bottlenecks could slow how quickly businesses adopt AI. But while both could weigh on the AI theme in the near term, they don’t necessarily undermine the longer-term opportunity.

I’m Evy Hambro, Head of the Global Resources and Real Assets Team. It’s the week of November 16th. Here are three things you need to know, and one you don’t. First up.Commodities, can’t build anything without them. For too many years commodities have been forgotten about. And, as a result of that, not enough attention has been applied to supply chains of the commodities relative to their use. There are opportunities here for all stakeholders, not just investors. Normally, when you go into a commodity cycle you have many years of positive returns. We think we are in the first quarter a new commodity cycle. Number two.Commodity companies deliver exposure to commodity prices. The second element is, what does the company do with the money it makes from producing a commodity? What the companies have got right since the bottom in 2016 is rebalancing and sharing returns with their investors. Commodity equities come with higher volatility, but the advantages in our views outweigh the disadvantages. The prospect for dividends, growth, exploration success, and M&A brings an element of upside other forms of commodity exposure do not. Which brings us to.People are turning back to gold as a source of diversification and wealth preservation. Think about it tangibly. Somebody who had a wallet full of European currency 24 years ago. Looking at that wallet today, those paper currencies, those Portuguese escudos and German marks, are worthless. If they had the same amount of money in gold coins, they probably would be worth more than what they could have bought back then. And that is one of the best examples of how gold can hold its purchasing power through time.

articles.link_title: Fixed Income Outlook Market Insights Fixed Income Outlook Oct 21, 2026 | By BlackRock Similar yields can carry very different risks. Explore how investors can capture income while being deliberate about risk.
articles.title: Q4 2026 Fixed Income Outlook | BlackRock
articles.excerpt: Higher yields have changed the fixed income opportunity. More of a portfolio's potential return can come from income, even as persistent inflation tests bonds' traditional diversification role and diverging economic cycles create different investment conditions across markets. The challenge is no longer simply finding yield, but understanding which risks investors are being paid to take. Income may be abundant, but it is not interchangeable; similar yields can carry very different risks. With policy rates and longer-term yields moving higher, investors are weighing how much risk higher rates pose to different parts of the economy. Growth remains resilient overall, but rate sensitivity varies significantly across sectors and households, while some inflation pressures are less responsive to rates. Today’s starting yields may allow investors to generate attractive income without reaching as far for it. Investors are questioning what is keeping long-term yields elevated and what that means for bonds in portfolios. Inflation is only part of the answer: stronger nominal growth, greater competition for capital and diminished diversification benefits are also contributing to higher yields. That combination strengthens fixed income’s role as a source of income, even as persistent inflation makes its diversification benefits more conditional. Higher European bond yields have improved the income opportunity, but tighter spreads leave less room for broad spread compression to drive returns. That shifts the focus toward relative value across corporate issuers and capital structures, while diverging fiscal and political paths create different considerations for sovereign investors.
